title: Why Did God Allow Sin?
hook: If God made us limited and bound to fail, can He punish us forever for it?
tldr: God created humans good, not perfect: finite in knowledge and emotion, with free will, so mistakes were inevitable. Sin is no Plan B but part of a designed learning journey toward understanding love, grace and forgiveness. Torturing people forever for the imperfection God built in is illogical and unethical.
big_idea: Created good, not perfect: sin is part of our growing, not grounds for torture.

points.title: A sick escape-room game
points.text: Threatening to burn someone unless they solve an escape room is cruel, yet newborns are said to face eternal hellfire unless they figure out a truth hidden from most people and cultures.

points.title: Good is not perfect
points.text: God called creation tov, good: fit for its purpose, not tamim, perfect. Finite humans with free will and limited knowledge inevitably make mistakes.

points.title: God has no Plan B
points.text: Genesis 3 was not a backup plan. As light is known through darkness, love, grace and forgiveness are only truly understood in the face of sin.

points.title: No pain, no gain
points.text: Sin harms, but it also prompts reflection, repentance, humility and empathy. Societies learned from slavery and trafficking; constraints and trauma can even spark creativity.

points.title: Limits make us need each other
points.text: Finite capacities are deliberate: they foster interdependence, relationships, free will and real character growth, which perfect beings with predetermined outcomes would lack.

points.title: A healer, not a disgusted judge
points.text: Sin cannot harm God, so He never turns away from sinners. Like Jesus touching the sick, God engages and restores rather than abhorring us or abusing us forever.

sections.h: The escape room and the hidden truth
sections.summary: Opening with The Human League's song Human: born to make mistakes. Imagine putting someone in an escape room and burning it unless they solve it: a sick game. Yet newborns are said to be destined for hellfire unless they figure it out. If life's purpose is avoiding hell, why hide that truth from almost everyone, favor cultures valuing one text, and require literal reading when many read it metaphorically? And deeper: what would a world without sin look like? Could it exist?

sections.h: Sin is part of the human learning experience
sections.summary: King David praised God's forgiveness and grace in his Psalms only after he sinned, not before. Forgiveness, grace and compassion learned only in theory are limited; they must be experienced emotionally. So human experience would be lacking, even impossible, without sin. This does not call sin good; it deduces sin is inherent to learning. The universe is no Plan B after Genesis 3 but a wise God's design. Condemning imperfect humans is like condemning a fish for not climbing a tree.

sections.h: Imperfect People in an Imperfect World
sections.summary: What is created good is not necessarily perfect. God is perfect and lacks nothing, but made humans with finite physical, mental and emotional capacities that grow but never reach perfection, so mistakes and wrong choices follow. Even self-centeredness is not purely evil: it is partly needed for survival, becoming sinful when it harms others. These imperfections serve a profound purpose in the divine blueprint, and this chapter asks why an omnipotent, omniscient God would build them in.

sections.h: Tov versus tamim: good, not perfect
sections.summary: God saw all he made was very good. The Hebrew tov means pleasing or beneficial, fulfilling its purpose well, not moral perfection. Perfect is tamim: completeness, wholeness, blamelessness, used in other contexts. A perfect creation could not have contained an evil entity in Eden. Scripture calls creation good, never perfect. Earthquakes, volcanoes and hurricanes cause damage yet sustain life: volcanoes create fertile land, hurricanes distribute heat. Bad events fit within a good creation.

sections.h: Only God is perfect and unchanging
sections.summary: Perfection is defined by God: omniscient, omnipresent, omnipotent, omnibenevolent. Even all knowledge would leave humans short of the other divine traits, so Adam and Eve were not created perfect but finite and limited in thought and decision-making. God's perfection means no change in His being, attributes or decrees; any change, better or worse, implies imperfection. Adam and Eve could learn and grow, so they were good, not perfect, with free will that, with limited knowledge, inevitably led to sin.

sections.h: The Meaning and Purpose of Life
sections.summary: Why believe life's purpose is mainly escaping eternal punishment? A more meaningful view: life is a journey of learning and growing in understanding of ourselves, of God's nature and, ultimately, of love. Here sin plays a paradoxical role. Love, grace and compassion can only truly be understood and appreciated in the face of sin. How else could Adam and Eve experience the full depth of God's love, grace and forgiveness without their sin?

The Augustinian-Calvinist view treats Genesis 3 as God's Plan B, triggered by disobedience. Instead, sin serves a purpose. Just as light is appreciated through darkness and warmth through cold, we must encounter evil to understand God's goodness, grace and kindness. This frees us from an anxious, unreachable pursuit of perfection toward the attainable goal of maturity and growth. Perfection will come, but not in this lifetime.

Sin brings pain: it destroys goodness, distorts relationships, erodes trust and spirals into guilt or vengeance. Yet it also opens room for creativity, growth and maturity. Humans are not robots; machines cannot sin. Each misstep invites reflection, mirrors our fallibility and need for justice, grace and divine guidance, and leads to repentance, seeking forgiveness from God and others, humility, empathy and compassion. Societies recognized the evil of slavery and child trafficking and banned them; individuals gain wisdom and godlier traits.

Clinical psychologist Jordan Peterson suggests adversity may be the greatest catalyst for growth, wisdom and creativity. He cites psychologist Hans Isaac's book Genius: early trauma predicts later creativity, though also catastrophic adult lives. There is no reason to be creative without a problem to solve, and laissez-faire parenting does not produce it; creativity emerges under serious constraints. Painful experiences shape our grasp of justice, empathy, mercy, grace, redemption and divine love, deepening faith and spiritual maturity.

sections.h: The Divine Intent Behind Human Limitations
sections.summary: God is perfect partly through omniscience, yet made humans finite, emotionally driven and thus bound to sin: we are born imperfect. Punishing people forever for how their Creator made them is like punishing a fish for not climbing trees or killing your children for botching your taxes. Limits are deliberate: they foster interdependence, since perfect beings would need no one. Relationships teach love, sacrifice, humility and patience. Limitations also make free will and genuine character development possible.

God could have downloaded all knowledge into us but gave only basic instincts, so we learn progressively through experience, and painful experience builds character, perhaps preparing us for the next world. Unlike AI, Siri or Alexa, humans feel pain and sorrow. Without sin we would not need forgiveness, and without forgiveness we could not grasp love's depth: whoever is forgiven little loves little. Mistakes and forgiveness deepen our grasp of love, grace, compassion and justice.

sections.h: All made new; God is not threatened by sin
sections.summary: We all at times become tools of evil, and sin destroys everything. But the Bible promises new bodies and a new earth, so we can forgive even someone who killed us. Sin's hopelessness shows we need a redeemer greater than ourselves; tying inevitable sin to hellfire is erroneous. Sin can hinder our relationship with God, but unlike people who cancel us, God is not harmed or intimidated by sin. A physician who despises patients cannot heal; Jesus touched sinners.

Since humans were created with inherent limitations, not perfection, judging them by absolute perfection is unreasonable. Claims that God only accepts absolute perfection, or that He abhors us and cannot stand to look at us, are irrational. Eternal torture for intrinsic imperfection is illogical and unethical. Such ideas portray God as a cruel, abusive tyrant rather than a loving Father, undermining the biblical picture of a compassionate, forgiving Creator.

mythfact.myth: God created Adam and Eve perfect, and sin ruined the plan.
mythfact.fact: Scripture calls creation good, never perfect. Adam and Eve were finite, able to learn and grow, and sin was no Plan B.

mythfact.myth: God cannot look at sinners and finds them loathsome.
mythfact.fact: Sin poses no threat to God. Jesus touched the sick and sinners to heal them; God's approach is engagement and restoration.

mythfact.myth: The purpose of life is to avoid eternal punishment.
mythfact.fact: Life's purpose is a journey of learning about ourselves, God's nature and, ultimately, the essence of love.

quotes.text: Condemning humans to eternal torture in Hellfire for not being perfect like God is akin to condemning a fish for its inability to climb a tree.
Our universe is not some “Plan B" that God devised in response to the events of Genesis 3.
Creativity emerges when you put serious constraints on things.

verses.role: Creation called very good, tov, never perfect.
The fall: not God's Plan B but part of a purposeful design.
God does not change; His perfection is unchanging.
Whoever has been forgiven little loves little: forgiveness teaches love.
Perfection will come, but not in this lifetime.
All things made new, grounding our forgiveness of others.
New bodies promised, so no harm done to us is final.

quiz.q: What does the Hebrew word tov in Genesis mean?
options: Good, fulfilling its intended purpose well
quiz.why: Tov means pleasing or beneficial; the word for perfect, tamim, is not used of creation.

quiz.q: When did King David write Psalms praising God's forgiveness?
quiz.why: David knew forgiveness by experiencing it; virtues like grace must be lived, not only learned in theory.

quiz.q: Why did God make humans finite, according to this view?
options: To foster growth, interdependence and free will
quiz.why: Limitations make us need one another, allow genuine choice and character growth, and teach love through relationships.

reflect: What have your own mistakes taught you about forgiveness that you could never have learned in theory?
